artiest/cappella-romana-en-alexander-lin.text:
Cappella Romana is a vocal ensemble founded in 1991 in Portland, Oregon. The name means Roman Chapel and refers to the medieval Greek idea of the Roman oikoumene, the inhabited world, which included Rome and Western Europe but also the Byzantine Empire, with Constantinople as the New Rome. The choir is known for its exploration of the music of the Eastern Orthodox tradition. Its music director is Alexander Lingas, a musicologist at City University in London who specialised in Byzantine music. Guest artists regularly take part, among them Ivan Moody and Vladimir Morosan.

The ensemble contributed to exhibitions at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York and the J. Paul Getty Museum in Los Angeles. In 2002 it performed Passion and Resurrection by Ivan Moody, and in 2014 it gave the world premiere in Portland of Passion Week, a choral work from 1923 by Maximilian Steinberg. From 2010 it took part in a Stanford University research project on the acoustics of the Hagia Sophia in Istanbul.

On the 2019 album Lost Voices of Hagia Sophia, those acoustics were recreated with digital techniques, so that Byzantine chant sounds the way it might have sounded in the church a thousand years ago, even though the recording was made in a studio in California. In this way the ensemble makes music from a distant past audible, and shows that space and sound belong together. In School of Rock the choir represents the early church music of the East, with, among other pieces, a Cherubic Hymn and a chant by Kassia.
artiest/cappella-romana-en-alexander-lin.listen: Listen to Lord, the Woman Found in Many Sins by Kassia. Notice the single melodic line of the singing, the long, slow phrases and how the reverberation of the space carries the sound.

artiest/cardi-b.text:
Cardi B is the stage name of Belcalis Marlenis Almánzar, an American rapper born in 1992 in Washington Heights in Manhattan and raised in the South Bronx. Her father is Dominican and her mother is from Trinidad. Her stage name is derived from Bacardi, a type of rum that used to be her nickname. She attended a high school for performing arts and technology and worked at a supermarket at seventeen. Her music career began in 2016, with two mixtapes.

Her first studio album, Invasion of Privacy, was released in 2018. It entered at number one on the Billboard 200 and became the best-selling and most highly certified female rap album of the twenty-first century. With it, Cardi B became the first solo artist to win a Grammy for Best Rap Album. Bodak Yellow and I Like It both reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100. Girls Like You from 2018 was her third number one in the United States. The collaboration WAP followed later, the only female rap collaboration to debut at the top of the Hot 100, and then Up. Her second album, Am I the Drama? from 2025, made her the only female rapper whose first two albums both debuted at number one on the Billboard 200.

Her music stands out for an energetic flow and outspoken lyrics. Cardi B was recognised for increasing the visibility of female rappers in popular music, and in 2018 Time named her one of the hundred most influential people in the world.
artiest/cardi-b.listen: Listen to Bodak Yellow and notice her flow. Hear how she raps in a sharp, rhythmic voice over a bare, heavy beat.

artiest/carl-hogan.text:
Carl Hogan was an American jazz and rhythm-and-blues guitarist and bassist. He was born in 1917, possibly in Louina, Alabama, and grew up in various places in the southern United States; his father was a preacher. According to other sources he grew up in St. Louis. He played guitar and bass in the Jeter-Pillars Orchestra and in the orchestra of George Hudson.

He then joined Louis Jordan and his Tympany Five, at first as a temporary bassist. With that band he played on many well-known recordings, such as Choo Choo Ch'Boogie, Ain't Nobody Here But Us Chickens, Let the Good Times Roll and Open the Door, Richard. He also appeared in Jordan's films. He stayed with the group until 1949. Jordan's music was swinging jump blues: short, cheerful and made for dancing, one of the forerunners of rock 'n' roll.

Hogan's most important moment comes in Ain't That Just Like a Woman (They'll Do It Every Time) from 1946. On it he played a short guitar riff that later returned almost note for note as the opening of Chuck Berry's Johnny B. Goode from 1958. Berry himself named Hogan, alongside T-Bone Walker and Charlie Christian, as one of his sources. In this way an almost unknown accompanist became the man behind perhaps the most famous guitar intro in rock 'n' roll. Hogan died in St. Louis in 1977.
artiest/carl-hogan.listen: Listen to Ain't That Just Like a Woman (They'll Do It Every Time) by Louis Jordan and then, straight afterwards, to the start of Johnny B. Goode by Chuck Berry. Notice Hogan's guitar riff at the beginning and how Berry takes it over.

artiest/carl-maria-von-weber.text:
Carl Maria von Weber (1786 to 1826) was a German composer, conductor, pianist, guitarist and critic of the late Classical and early Romantic periods. He was born in Eutin, the eldest child of Franz Anton von Weber and the Viennese singer Genovefa Brenner. His father constantly moved the family around between Hamburg, Salzburg, Freiberg, Augsburg and Vienna. As a result Weber had many teachers, among them Michael Haydn and Georg Joseph Vogler. The aristocratic von was an affectation of his father's.

Weber is known above all for his operas. His most important are Silvana in 1810, Abu Hassan in 1811, Der Freischütz in 1821, Euryanthe in 1823 and Oberon in 1826. Der Freischütz is regarded as one of the most important German operas and made German Romantic opera great. His influence on Marschner, Meyerbeer and Wagner was considerable. He also wrote two symphonies, clarinet concertos, a bassoon concerto, a horn concertino, piano concertos and piano pieces such as Invitation to the Dance. Much of his clarinet music was written for the virtuoso Heinrich Baermann.

His piano music inspired Mendelssohn, Chopin and Liszt. With operas full of nature, folk tales and supernatural forces, Weber laid the foundation for Romantic music in Germany, a current that still resonates in the twentieth century in music of fairy tales, suspense and landscape.
artiest/carl-maria-von-weber.listen: Listen to the overture to Der Freischütz. Notice the horns that evoke a woodland atmosphere and how the piece alternates between dark tension and light, cheerful melodies.

artiest/carl-orff.text:
Carl Orff (1895 to 1982) was a German composer and music educator, born in Munich into a military family that was also learned and musical. He attended the Akademie der Tonkunst in his home city and at first wrote songs and orchestral works. In 1936 he completed Carmina Burana for voices and large orchestra, setting medieval poems from a collection of the same name. The premiere was an immediate great success, and Orff felt that here, for the first time, he had done exactly what he wanted. After the Second World War the popularity of the work grew enormously. His later pieces, such as the other two parts of the triptych Trionfi, of which Carmina Burana is the first part, received much less attention. He also wrote Catulli Carmina and Trionfo di Afrodite.

Orff also became influential as an educator. With colleagues such as Gunild Keetman he developed the Orff Schulwerk, a collection of principles for enabling every child to learn music like a new language, in a relaxed environment, with simple instruments and specially written music. His relationship with the Third Reich has been examined by many: he was a member of the Reichsmusikkammer, but not of the Nazi Party, and after the war he was given permission to make music again without restriction.

Carmina Burana sounds like a rhythmic, driving choral work with repeated patterns and hard percussion accents. That direct power later made it a favourite with makers of film, advertising and pop music.
artiest/carl-orff.listen: Listen to the opening chorus of Carmina Burana. Notice the repeating rhythms, the percussion accents and how chorus and orchestra together create a grand, menacing sound.

artiest/carl-sigman.text:
Carl Sigman (1909 to 2000) was an American songwriter, born in Crown Heights in Brooklyn into a Jewish-American family. He studied law and passed the bar exam, but, encouraged by his friend Johnny Mercer, chose to write songs instead. In the Second World War he was awarded the Bronze Star for his service in Africa.

Sigman also wrote melodies, but was above all a lyricist. He worked with Bob Hilliard, Bob Russell, Jimmy van Heusen and Duke Ellington. In the big-band era he wrote material for orchestras such as those of Glenn Miller and Guy Lombardo, including Pennsylvania 6-5000. His songs also became hits for singers: My Heart Cries for You was recorded in 1951 by Dinah Shore, Guy Mitchell and Vic Damone. Ebb Tide was a hit for Frank Chacksfield and reached the American top ten in 1965 with the Righteous Brothers. In 1958 Tommy Edwards had a number one with It's All in the Game, with Sigman's lyrics set to music that Charles Gates Dawes had written in 1912. He also wrote English lyrics for songs from other languages, such as Answer Me, Till, The Day the Rains Came, You're My World and What Now My Love? He became best known for Where Do I Begin, the theme song of Love Story.

In 1972 Sigman was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame. He shows how important a lyricist is to the great standards of popular music.
artiest/carl-sigman.listen: Listen to Ebb Tide in the version by the Righteous Brothers and pay attention to the words. Hear how words about the sea and the waves make the singing and the accompaniment surge together.

artiest/carl-stalling.text: Carl Stalling (1891–1972) was a cinema organist in Kansas City, where he accompanied silent films. Walt Disney knew him from that city and in 1928 asked him to create the sound for his first Mickey Mouse films. He did not score Steamboat Willie himself, but he did the sound versions of Plane Crazy and The Gallopin' Gaucho. He proposed the Silly Symphonies and wrote The Skeleton Dance (1929). From 1936 to 1958 he worked at Warner Bros. on the Looney Tunes. There his music followed every movement to the second, and he quoted well-known songs at lightning speed. Every gag had its own musical wink. His work was rediscovered in 1990 through the album The Carl Stalling Project.
artiest/carl-stalling.listen: Notice the rapid changes of style and tempo, the quoted songs and how every bang or fall gets its own musical accent.

artiest/carla-bley.text: Carla Bley, from Oakland, worked as a young woman as a cigarette seller at the jazz club Birdland. There she heard the music she wanted to write. In the early 1960s her pieces were played by Paul Bley, to whom she was married, and by George Russell and Jimmy Giuffre. In 1964 she was one of the founders of the Jazz Composers Guild. With Charlie Haden she created the Liberation Music Orchestra and with her later partner Michael Mantler the Jazz Composer's Orchestra. Escalator over the Hill (1971) is a jazz opera of almost two hours with lyrics by Paul Haines. Her music is often humorous and draws on the tango, marches and hymns.
artiest/carla-bley.listen: Notice how the orchestra changes style: theatre, jazz and rock all mixed together.

artiest/carleen-anderson.text:
Carleen Anderson is an American singer, composer and musician, born in 1957 in Houston, Texas, and living in the United Kingdom since 1990. She was already singing solo for the congregation at the age of three. At seven she composed songs, played the piano by ear and led the choir of the Anderson Memorial Church of God in Christ, where her grandfather was the preacher. Her aunt Betty Faye Anderson, a gospel singer and soprano with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, influenced her voice. Later she studied classical music and jazz in Los Angeles, and as a single mother of a son she worked as a tutor.

In England she was the singer, composer and musician of the Young Disciples. Her solo career began in 1992. On Virgin Records' Circa label, the EP Dusky Sappho appeared in 1993, and in 1994 her debut album True Spirit, with the singles Mama Said, Let It Last and Nervous Breakdown. The second album, Blessed Burden from 1998, had success with Woman in Me and a version of Paul McCartney's Maybe I'm Amazed. Alberta's Granddaughter followed in 2002, Soul Providence in 2005 and Cage Street Memorial, The Pilgrimage in 2016. She often collaborated with others and wrote futuristic operas.

Her voice comes from gospel and soul, and found a home in England in acid jazz and dance music. She shows how the singing tradition of the church and modern British club music can strengthen each other.
artiest/carleen-anderson.listen: Listen to Mama Said from True Spirit and pay attention to her voice. Hear how gospel and soul resonate in her singing over a modern rhythm.

artiest/carlo-gesualdo.text:
Carlo Gesualdo da Venosa (1566 to 1613) was an Italian nobleman and composer. He was Prince of Venosa and Count of Conza, but is better known for his madrigals and church music, written in a chromatic language that would not be heard again until the end of the nineteenth century. His family had acquired the principality of Venosa in 1560. He was probably born in Venosa. His uncle was Carlo Borromeo, the future saint Charles Borromeo. His mother died when he was seven. After the death of his brother Luigi in 1584 he became heir and gave up an ecclesiastical career. In 1586 he married his cousin Maria d'Avalos. He killed her and her aristocratic lover when he caught them together.

From an early age Gesualdo was wholly devoted to music and played the lute. His madrigals appeared in six books, from Libro I to Libro VI, the last of which dates from 1613. He also wrote sacred music, including Tenebrae responsories for Holy Week, motets and the Sacrae Cantiones.

The sound is remarkable: sudden, sharp turns in harmony and tempo that follow the words of the text. As a result Gesualdo is regarded as an outsider of the late Renaissance, whose music has since been rediscovered by composers and listeners as surprisingly modern.
artiest/carlo-gesualdo.listen: Listen to a madrigal from Libro VI or to a Tenebrae responsory. Notice the sudden, strange chord changes and how the voices change mood, sometimes slowly, sometimes quickly.

artiest/carlo-karges.text:
Carlo Karges was a German guitarist and songwriter. He was born in 1951 in Hamburg and grew up there with his mother. As a schoolboy he began playing the guitar and writing his own songs. He played in groups such as Tomorrow's Gift and Release Music Orchestra, and in 1971 he was one of the founders of Novalis, in which he played guitar and keyboards.

In 1981 he formed the band named after her, Nena, with the singer Gabriele Kerner, who went by the name Nena, and with Rolf Brendel, Jürgen Dehmel and Uwe Fahrenkrog-Petersen. The group made energetic, German-language pop music with guitars and synthesizers. Karges wrote the lyrics of the band's best-known song, 99 Luftballons, which was released in 1983. It became a huge hit, also outside Germany, and later also appeared in an English version, 99 Red Balloons.

He got the idea for the lyrics in 1982 at a Rolling Stones concert in the Waldbühne in West Berlin, where balloons were released into the sky. Karges wondered what East German or Soviet troops would do if those balloons drifted over the Berlin Wall. This gave rise to a song about a great war that begins with a misunderstanding over a cloud of balloons. The song brought the fear of the Cold War into the charts. Karges died in Hamburg in 2002, at the age of 50.
artiest/carlo-karges.listen: Listen to 99 Luftballons by Nena. Notice how the song begins calmly and then speeds up, just as in the story an innocent cloud of balloons ends in war.

artiest/carlo-maria-giulini.text:
Carlo Maria Giulini (1914 to 2005) was an Italian conductor, born in Barletta in Apulia and raised in Bolzano, where the local music sounded mainly Austrian and Tyrolean. He was given a violin at the age of five. At sixteen he went to the Conservatorio Santa Cecilia in Rome, where he studied viola and conducting. He won a place in the orchestra of the Accademia Nazionale di Santa Cecilia. Two years later he won a conducting competition, but could not make use of the prize because, although a pacifist, he had to join the army. At the end of the war he went into hiding and married Marcella, with whom he remained until her death in 1995.

After the liberation in 1944 he conducted the first concert of the then Augusteo orchestra after Fascism, and he soon received more invitations, among others from the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, the Philharmonia Orchestra in London, the Los Angeles Philharmonic and the Vienna Philharmonic. His career lasted 54 years and ended in 1998. Among his recordings are Le nozze di Figaro in 1961, Verdi's Requiem in 1964, Don Carlo in 1971, Dvořák's Ninth Symphony in 1977 and Debussy's La Mer.

Giulini was known for his careful, deep and often slow approach to the repertoire, from opera to symphony. He shows that a conductor does not merely perform the music, but gives it time and breath.
artiest/carlo-maria-giulini.listen: Listen to Debussy's La Mer under Giulini. Notice how the waves of the orchestra slowly build up and how each instrumental group is given its own colour.

artiest/carlos-gardel.text:
Carlos Gardel was born in Toulouse in 1890 as Charles Romuald Gardès, the son of an unmarried laundress. Around 1893 his mother left with him for Buenos Aires, where she did French-style ironing in the San Nicolás district. He grew up speaking Spanish and became Carlos, or Carlitos. A disputed theory holds that he was born in Tacuarembó, Uruguay, but research into the French baptismal and birth registers confirms Toulouse.

Gardel became the most important figure in the history of the tango and one of the most influential singers of popular music in the first half of the twentieth century. He was sometimes called a baritone, sometimes a tenor, because of his wide range, and was known for his rich voice and dramatic phrasing. Together with the lyricist Alfredo Le Pera he wrote several classic tangos. His nicknames included El Zorzal, the song thrush, and the King of the Tango.

He was killed in a plane crash in 1935, at the height of his career, and became a tragic hero mourned throughout Latin America. For many he embodies the soul of the tango. Por una Cabeza from 1935 is among his last work. His recordings continue to appear on new albums to this day, including in new arrangements.
artiest/carlos-gardel.listen: Listen to Por una Cabeza. Notice the warm, smooth voice and how Gardel stretches the phrases and holds them back again, as if he were telling a story.

artiest/carlos-kleiber.text:
Carlos Kleiber (1930 to 2004) was a German-born Austrian conductor who is widely regarded as one of the greatest conductors of all time. He was born in Berlin, the son of the famous conductor Erich Kleiber and the American Ruth Goodrich. In 1935 the family emigrated to Buenos Aires and Karl became Carlos. His father did not want him to become a musician. Carlos first studied chemistry in Zürich, but chose music after all. In 1954 he conducted for the first time, the operetta Gasparone in Potsdam. He was then Kapellmeister in Düsseldorf and Duisburg, in Zürich and, until 1973, in Stuttgart, his last permanent post. Later he often conducted at the Bavarian State Opera in Munich.

He was known as a perfectionist who demanded long rehearsals. What he finally let the audience hear combined precision with passionate spontaneity. Kleiber disliked recording and therefore left little behind, including Der Freischütz in 1985, La traviata in 1985, Tristan und Isolde and above all symphonies by Beethoven and Brahms. His New Year's Concert of 1992 can also be heard on record. He was most at home in the Romantic repertoire.

The small number of recordings made Kleiber a legend among musicians and music lovers. He shows that a performance is about preparation, feeling and the freedom of the moment.
artiest/carlos-kleiber.listen: Listen to his recording of Der Freischütz. Notice the energy and precision of the orchestra, and hear how the conductor lets the tension build without the piece becoming heavy.

artiest/carmen-miranda.text:
Carmen Miranda, whose real name was Maria do Carmo Miranda da Cunha, was born in 1909 in a village in the north of Portugal and grew up in Brazil. As a young woman she designed clothes and hats in a boutique, before making her debut as a singer in 1929 with the composer Josué de Barros. Her 1930 recording of Taí (Pra Você Gostar de Mim), written by Joubert de Carvalho, made her famous in Brazil as the foremost interpreter of the samba.

In the 1930s she sang on Brazilian radio and appeared in five chanchadas, films about Brazilian music, dance and carnival. The 1939 film Banana da Terra gave her the image of the Baiana, inspired by Afro-Brazilians from Bahia. In 1939 the Broadway producer Lee Shubert offered her a contract, and in 1940 her first Hollywood film followed, Down Argentine Way. Her exuberant clothing, with the fruit hats, and her Brazilian-Portuguese accent became her trademark. In 1941 she was the first Latin American star to leave her handprints at Grauman's Chinese Theatre. Between 1940 and 1953 she made fourteen Hollywood films.

After the war her popularity declined. She was irritated by the stereotypical image of the Brazilian bombshell and tried to break free from it. Even so, she made Brazilian music known and increased American attention to Latin American culture. She is regarded as a forerunner of the Brazilian tropicália of the 1960s and died in 1955.
artiest/carmen-miranda.listen: Listen to Taí (Pra Você Gostar de Mim). Notice the playful rhythm of the samba and how Miranda almost speaks the words, with a great deal of rhythmic verve.

artiest/carmen-twillie.text:
Carmen Twillie is an American actress and singer. She is a good friend of Tommy Morgan and appeared as guest alto soloist with his choir. She is best known as the voice singing Circle of Life at the beginning of the Disney film The Lion King from 1994, a song by Elton John and Tim Rice.

She also sang Stormella in the Christmas film Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer: The Movie from 1998 and was one of the singers in Cats Don't Dance from 1997. In the stop-motion film The Nightmare Before Christmas from 1993 she voiced a few minor roles. She also worked on an episode of the series Chowder.

Twillie is also a backing singer and sang on albums by Celine Dion, Whitney Houston, Dionne Warwick and Pink Floyd, for the album A Momentary Lapse of Reason from 1987. In this way her voice can be heard on many records, even when her name is not on the front. That fits the work of backing singers, who contribute a great deal to the sound of pop and film without being the face of the record.
artiest/carmen-twillie.listen: Listen to the beginning of Circle of Life from The Lion King. Notice her powerful alto voice, which sets the opening sound before the choir and the orchestra come in.

artiest/carmen-twillie-en-lebo-m.text:
Carmen Twillie and Lebo M. are the voices that carried the opening of the Disney film The Lion King in 1994. Twillie is an American actress and singer, an alto voice known as a longtime friend of Tommy Morgan and as a guest soloist with his choir. In the film she sang Circle of Life, the song by Elton John and Tim Rice, at the start of the film. Lebo M., a South African composer, sang the Zulu invocation with which the song opens.

Besides this song, Twillie was active as a voice actress and backing singer. In 1997 she sang in the animated film Cats Don't Dance, in 1998 she was the singing voice of Stormella in Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer: The Movie, and she did minor voice roles in The Nightmare Before Christmas from 1993. She was also a backing singer on albums by Celine Dion, Whitney Houston, Dionne Warwick and Pink Floyd, on their album A Momentary Lapse of Reason from 1987.

Circle of Life shows how pop music and film music came together in the 1990s: a pop song by two British makers, sung by an American soul voice, over an opening scene that begins with an African vocal group. That made it one of the best-known openings of an animated film.
artiest/carmen-twillie-en-lebo-m.listen: Listen to Circle of Life. Notice the way the song begins with the Zulu invocation by Lebo M. and how Twillie's voice then opens the song, accompanied by choir and orchestra.

artiest/carmine-coppola.text:
Carmine Coppola (1910 to 1991) was an American composer, flautist, pianist and songwriter, born in New York to Italian immigrants from Bernalda in Basilicata. His brother was the opera conductor and composer Anton Coppola. Carmine studied at Juilliard, later at the Manhattan School of Music and privately with Joseph Schillinger. In the 1940s he played under Arturo Toscanini in the NBC Symphony Orchestra. In 1951 he left the orchestra to concentrate on composing. He worked mainly as a conductor on Broadway and elsewhere and wrote additional music for Finian's Rainbow, directed by his son Francis Ford Coppola.

He is the father of the director Francis Ford Coppola, of August Coppola and of Talia Shire, and the grandfather of, among others, Nicolas Cage and Sofia Coppola. For his son he supplied music for films such as The Godfather, The Godfather Part II, Apocalypse Now, The Outsiders, The Black Stallion and The Godfather Part III. He contributed to the music of the wedding scene in The Godfather from 1972 and worked on the score of The Godfather Part II from 1974. He won an Academy Award and a Golden Globe for best original film score, and received nominations for a BAFTA and a Grammy. Albums such as The Godfather Suite from 1977, The Black Stallion from 1980 and Napoleon from 1989 showcase his work.

Coppola shows how a classically trained musician in a family firm of filmmakers could shape the sound of an era, with music that evokes atmosphere and ancestry at the same time.
artiest/carmine-coppola.listen: Listen to the wedding music or the main theme from The Godfather Suite. Notice the Italian, danceable character and how a simple melody evokes a whole world.

artiest/carol-kaye.text:
Carol Kaye is an American musician, born in 1935 in Everett, Washington, as Carol Smith. Her parents were professional musicians and her father was a jazz trombonist in big bands. At thirteen she was given a steel-string guitar by her mother. In the 1950s she played bebop guitar with groups in Los Angeles, including with Jack Sheldon and Teddy Edwards, and with the orchestra of Henry Busse.

In 1957 she began studio work. Through a contact at Gold Star Studios she worked for the producers Phil Spector and Brian Wilson. When a bassist failed to show up at a session in 1963, she switched to bass guitar and quickly became one of the most in-demand session musicians of the 1960s. She belongs to the Wrecking Crew, the group of Los Angeles studio musicians, and is estimated to have played on ten thousand recordings in a career of more than sixty-five years. At the end of the 1960s she also began playing on film music, chiefly for Quincy Jones and Lalo Schifrin, and wrote instruction books such as How To Play The Electric Bass. Under her own name The First Lady on Bass appeared in 1994 and Thumbs Up in 1999. In 2025 she was elected to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, but she declined the honour.

Kaye shows that the bass line carries the pop of the 1960s, even when her name is missing from the sleeve. Her mobile, melodic bass gave many records a character of their own.
artiest/carol-kaye.listen: Listen to a 1960s pop song from Los Angeles, such as a record by the Beach Boys, and listen only to the bass guitar. Hear how it does not merely follow the chords but plays a melody of its own.

artiest/carole-king.text:
Carole King was born in Manhattan in 1942 as Carol Joan Klein. In 1959 she married the lyricist Gerry Goffin. Together they wrote hit after hit for other artists in the early 1960s: King the music, Goffin the lyrics. Later King herself became one of the best-known singer-songwriters of the 1970s. In this way she bridges two ways of working: the hit factory, in which writers and singers were separate, and the artist who sings her own songs.

Will You Love Me Tomorrow (1960) became a number 1 for The Shirelles, The Loco-Motion a hit for Little Eva, and (You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman they wrote for Aretha Franklin. After her divorce from Goffin in 1968 King moved to Laurel Canyon in Los Angeles. She played in the trio The City and made the solo album Writer (1970). Then came Tapestry (1971), with her own piano as its foundation. The album spent fifteen weeks at number 1 in America, remained on the album chart for almost six years and won four Grammys. It's Too Late, with lyrics by Toni Stern, won the Grammy for Record of the Year.

On Tapestry King also sings her own versions of songs she had previously written for others, such as Will You Love Me Tomorrow and A Natural Woman. You've Got a Friend from the same album became a number 1 for James Taylor in 1971. In 1990 King was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a songwriter together with Goffin, and in 2021 once more as a performer. Since 2014 the Broadway musical Beautiful has told her life story.
artiest/carole-king.listen: It's Too Late (1971): alongside King's own piano you hear an electric piano played by Ralph Schuckett. Notice the two instrumental solos: electric guitar by Danny Kortchmar and soprano saxophone by Curtis Amy.

artiest/carolyn-franklin.text:
Carolyn Franklin (1944 to 1988) was an American singer and songwriter. She was born in Memphis, the youngest of six children of C.L. Franklin and Barbara Siggers Franklin. Shortly after her birth the family moved to Buffalo, and around 1946 it settled in Detroit. There Carolyn began singing in her father's New Bethel Baptist Church. Her sisters Erma and Aretha found success with secular music in the early 1960s, and Carolyn followed them. In 1963 she recorded for the first time.

From 1969 she recorded for RCA, until she left the music world in 1976. Releases under her own name include Baby Dynamite! in 1969, Chain Reaction and The First Time I Cried in 1970, I'd Rather Be Lonely in 1973 and If You Want Me in 1976. She and Erma did not match Aretha's success, and so Carolyn worked mainly behind the scenes as a songwriter, chiefly for Aretha. She wrote Ain't No Way, recorded in 1968, which reached the R&B top ten and the top twenty of the Billboard Hot 100. In 1973 came the ballad Angel, with Carolyn and Erma on backing vocals and a tribute from Aretha at the start. She also wrote Pullin' in 1970 with Jimmy Radcliffe and Aretha.

Carolyn Franklin still sang with Aretha now and then, including in the film The Blues Brothers in 1980. She died in 1988. Her work shows that behind a great soul voice there is often also a writer and backing singer.
artiest/carolyn-franklin.listen: Listen to Ain't No Way by Aretha Franklin, written by Carolyn. Notice the long, pleading quality of the singing and the backing voices that give the reply.

artiest/carpenters.text:
The Carpenters were an American duo of brother and sister: Karen (1950 to 1983) and Richard Carpenter (born in 1946). They were born in New Haven, Connecticut, and moved to Downey, California, in 1963. Richard took piano lessons and studied at California State University in Long Beach, while Karen learned to play the drums. In 1965 they performed together for the first time, with the jazz-oriented Richard Carpenter Trio and later the band Spectrum. In 1969 they signed to A&M Records as Carpenters.

Success came a year later with the singles (They Long to Be) Close to You and We've Only Just Begun. Their albums included Offering in 1969, Close to You in 1970, A Song for You in 1972, Horizon in 1975 and Made in America in 1981. They had three number one hits and five number two hits on the Billboard Hot 100, and fifteen number one hits on the Adult Contemporary chart. The duo's soft style grew out of Karen's alto voice and Richard's arrangements, compositions and harmonies. In the 1970s they toured relentlessly, which put them under pressure. In 1979 Richard took a year off because of an addiction to Quaaludes, and Karen suffered from anorexia nervosa. In 1983 Karen died of heart failure resulting from that illness, which brought a great deal of attention to eating disorders.

The Carpenters were leaders in soft rock and easy listening. Their smooth, warm sound shows how little it took to make a hit: a voice that sounds close by, strings and a simple melody.
artiest/carpenters.listen: Listen to We've Only Just Begun and pay attention to Karen's voice. Hear how low and close to the ear she sings and how the arrangement slowly grows larger.

artiest/carson-smith.text:
Carson Raymond Smith (1931 to 1997) was an American jazz double bassist, born in San Francisco. He was the older brother of the jazz musician and composer Putter Smith. His early work was in West Coast jazz: he played with Gerry Mulligan from 1952 to 1953, with Chet Baker from 1953 to 1955, with Russ Freeman and with Chico Hamilton. He also recorded with Clifford Brown and Dick Twardzik, and in 1956 accompanied Billie Holiday at Carnegie Hall.

In 1959 he toured with the orchestra of Stan Kenton and in 1960 he recorded with Charlie Barnet. In 1962 he moved to Los Angeles, where he played with Charlie Teagarden and Lionel Hampton. In 1964 he toured Japan with Georgie Auld. Later in the 1960s he played with Buddy Rich, Arno Marsh and Carl Fontana. In 1989 he worked on a reunion album with Chico Hamilton. Eventually he found a permanent post at the Four Queens Hotel in Las Vegas, where he accompanied visiting musicians such as Art Farmer, Lew Tabackin, Zoot Sims and Chet Baker. He died of cancer in Las Vegas at the age of 66.

Smith belongs to the bassists who carried the sound of West Coast jazz in the 1950s. A bassist like him seldom makes the headlines, but without his solid, precise accompaniment the soloists of that time could not have soared.
artiest/carson-smith.listen: Listen to a recording by Gerry Mulligan's quartet from 1952 or 1953 and focus on the double bass. Notice how it calmly maintains the chords while the horns follow one another.

artiest/carter-burwell.text: Carter Burwell was born in New York in 1955. He did not study composition but animation and electronic music, and worked as a computer programmer and in bands. In 1984 the brothers Joel and Ethan Coen asked him to score their debut Blood Simple. Since then he has written the music for almost all their films. Burwell often uses existing folk melodies as a basis. In Fargo (1996) he built the main theme on a Norwegian folk melody, played by a large orchestra with thundering drums. For Spike Jonze's Being John Malkovich (1999) he wrote strange, floating music. Todd Haynes's Carol (2015) sounds melancholy, with repeated figures in clarinet and strings. He also often works with the director Martin McDonagh.
artiest/carter-burwell.listen: Notice how a simple folk melody becomes almost menacing through repetition and a heavy orchestra.

artiest/cartola.text:
Cartola, whose real name was Angenor de Oliveira, was born in 1908 in the Catete district of Rio de Janeiro and was the eldest of eight children. His nickname, which means hat, came from the hat he wore as a bricklayer to protect his hair. As a child he watched his father play guitar and cavaquinho and was given a cavaquinho himself. In 1919 the family moved to Mangueira, then a small, growing favela, where his lifelong friend and regular writing partner Carlos Cachaça lived.

In 1928 Cartola helped to found the samba school Estação Primeira de Mangueira. He proposed that the colours green and pink of his earlier carnival group should also become those of the school. His work was popular in the 1930s. In the 1940s he disappeared from samba until 1956. In 1964 he opened the restaurant Zicartola with his wife Zica, where live samba was played. In 1974 he began recording solo albums, and in 1978 he gave his first solo concert, at the age of seventy. As Rosas Não Falam is on his 1976 album.

Cartola wrote more than five hundred songs, alone or with others. He is regarded as one of the most important figures in the development of samba, both as a composer and as a poet. His work shows that samba was not only party music, but also a form of poetry with melancholy.
artiest/cartola.listen: Listen to As Rosas Não Falam. Notice the soft voice, the accompaniment of guitar and cavaquinho and how the melody sounds sad, even though it is a samba.

artiest/cassandra-wilson.text: Cassandra Wilson, from Jackson, Mississippi, sang in the 1980s with Steve Coleman in the New York M-Base scene. She names Betty Carter as an important example, alongside Joni Mitchell. In 1993 she made Blue Light 'til Dawn for Blue Note, with blues by Robert Johnson, songs by Joni Mitchell and Van Morrison, and acoustic accompaniment without piano. The album was a great success. Her voice is low, dark and relaxed. On New Moon Daughter (1995) she sang, among other things, Strange Fruit and won a Grammy. She died in 2026 in Jackson.
artiest/cassandra-wilson.listen: Listen to the low, smoky voice above guitars and percussion.

artiest/cassius.text:
Cassius was a French duo active from 1988 to 2019, consisting of the producers Philippe Cerboneschi and Hubert Blanc-Francard, better known as Zdar and Boombass. They met in 1988 at the +XXX studios in Paris and first worked together on albums by the French hip-hop artist MC Solaar. In 1991 they started the project La Funk Mob and began to experiment more and more with electronic sounds. The duo is counted among the French touch movement, the French electronic music of the second half of the 1990s.

In 1996 they made their first house track under the name Cassius, Foxxy. After that they remixed for, among others, Air. In January 1999 Cassius 1999 appeared, their first real hit, which entered the British chart at number 7. The debut album 1999 followed, with Feeling For You and La Mouche. The second album Au Rêve came in 2002, with I'm a Woman featuring the singer Jocelyn Brown and The Sound of Violence. In 2006 came Toop Toop and the album 15 Again.

Outside Cassius, Zdar was a sought-after producer and sound engineer and recorded, among others, albums by Phoenix, Chromeo, Franz Ferdinand and the Beastie Boys. His own studio was called Motorbass. He died in Paris in 2019. The music of Cassius blends house and disco with funk and hip hop, and shows why the French electronic scene of those years gained such great influence.
artiest/cassius.listen: Listen to Cassius 1999. Notice the repeating, filtered loop and how the beat slowly builds up, as if the track were slowly warming up the dance floor.

artiest/cbc-symphony-orchestra.text:
The CBC Symphony Orchestra was a radio orchestra in Toronto, Canada, run in the 1950s and 1960s by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The orchestra was founded in 1952 and gave its first broadcast on 29 September 1952, with the Third Symphony by Jean Sibelius and the overture to Rossini's La Cenerentola. Geoffrey Waddington was the only music director, although conductors such as Jean-Marie Beaudet also had close ties with the orchestra. It consisted of eighty instrumentalists, about half of whom were also members of the Toronto Symphony Orchestra. Albert Pratz was concertmaster from 1953 to 1961.

The orchestra played weekly on CBC Radio and often appeared on CBC Television. It also travelled abroad, including to London, and played at the Inter-American Music Festival in 1961. Many performances were recorded by Radio Canada International and distributed outside Canada. The orchestra recorded with the Mendelssohn Choir, the CBC's Festival Singers and the pianist Glenn Gould. It also played and recorded a great deal of music by Igor Stravinsky, including the Symphony of Psalms, with Stravinsky himself conducting and Steven Staryk as concertmaster. Those recordings later appeared on albums such as Stravinsky Conducts Stravinsky.

In 1964 the orchestra was disbanded. It shows how radio in the mid-twentieth century brought classical music to a large audience.
artiest/cbc-symphony-orchestra.listen: Listen to the Symphony of Psalms in the recording under Stravinsky. Notice the choir and the wind instruments, because the piece leaves out the violins and violas and therefore sounds stark and solemn.

artiest/cecil-mcbee.text:
Cecil McBee is an American jazz bassist, born in 1935 in Tulsa, Oklahoma. At school he learned the clarinet, but at seventeen he switched to double bass and played in local nightclubs. He earned a music degree at Central State University in Ohio and for two years led the army band at Fort Knox. In 1959 he played with Dinah Washington and in 1962 he moved to Detroit, where in 1963 and 1964 he worked with Paul Winter's folk-rock ensemble.

His jazz career took off in the mid-1960s in New York. He played and recorded with important musicians, among them Miles Davis, Andrew Hill, Sam Rivers, Jackie McLean, Wayne Shorter, Charles Lloyd, Yusef Lateef, Keith Jarrett, Freddie Hubbard, Woody Shaw and Alice Coltrane. Under his own name he recorded only a handful of records, including Mutima in 1974, Alternate Spaces in 1979 and Unspoken in 1997. As a sideman he contributed to many classic jazz albums. In 1988 he won a Grammy for Blues for Coltrane: A Tribute to John Coltrane, together with Pharoah Sanders, David Murray, McCoy Tyner and Roy Haynes. In 1991 he was inducted into the Oklahoma Jazz Hall of Fame. He was artist in residence at Harvard and teaches at the New England Conservatory in Boston.

McBee is a bassist who above all carries other people's music, and in doing so gave the jazz of the 1960s and 1970s a broad, warm foundation.
artiest/cecil-mcbee.listen: Listen to a track by Alice Coltrane from the years 1969 to 1972 on which McBee plays. Notice the bass beneath the long, flowing lines of harp and piano and hear how he carries the movement.

artiest/cecil-taylor.text: The pianist Cecil Taylor, from New York, studied at the New England Conservatory and named Duke Ellington and Thelonious Monk as his most important examples in jazz. As early as 1956, before Ornette Coleman, he recorded music that left the boundaries of bebop behind. Taylor played the piano like a percussion instrument: clusters of notes, lightning-fast lines and eruptions of energy. He said he was playing 88 drums. On Unit Structures and Conquistador! (both 1966) his groups played long, layered compositions. He often gave solo concerts of more than an hour and worked with dancers and poets. He was also greatly appreciated in Europe.
artiest/cecil-taylor.listen: Listen to the piano as a percussion instrument: waves of sound instead of melody and accompaniment.

artiest/cecile-corbel.text:
Cécile Corbel is a French and Breton singer, harpist and composer, born in 1980 in Pont-Croix. As a child she travelled all over Brittany with her parents, who ran a travelling puppet theatre. She learned the guitar first and, as a teenager, discovered the Celtic harp at a concert by the Greek harpist Elisa Vellia, who later became her teacher. At eighteen she went to study in Paris, where she earned a master's degree in archaeology at the École du Louvre. She began performing in cafés and on the street and gave her first official concert in 2002.

In 2005 the EP Harpe celtique et chants du monde appeared, and in 2006 her first album, Songbook Vol. 1, with Breton, Welsh and Irish songs. She performed in many countries and shared the stage with, among others, Altan, Lúnasa and Alan Stivell. In 2009 she played Anne of Brittany in the rock opera Anne de Bretagne. Albums followed such as Songbook Vol. 2, Roses, La Fiancée, Vagabonde, Enfant du vent and Graal.

In 2010 she made the song for the Studio Ghibli film Arrietty. She had sent a CD of Songbook Vol. 2 to the studio, because she had been a fan for years. The producer Toshio Suzuki was looking for music with a Celtic colour, fell for her voice and the sound of the harp, and asked her to write the title song. Corbel sings in several languages, including French, Italian, Breton and English, and in this way brings the Celtic folk tradition to a large international audience.
artiest/cecile-corbel.listen: Listen to Arrietty's Song. Notice how the Celtic harp carries the song and how her voice floats above it, very light and soft.

artiest/cecile-mclorin-salvant.text: Cécile McLorin Salvant was born in Miami, the daughter of a Haitian father and a French mother. She studied classical singing and Baroque music in Aix-en-Provence and discovered jazz there. In 2010 she won the Thelonious Monk vocal competition. She names singers such as Sarah Vaughan and Bessie Smith as examples and sings old, often forgotten songs from vaudeville and the blues, alongside her own work. In doing so she critically shows how women are portrayed in those songs. She has won several Grammys and received a MacArthur fellowship in 2020.
artiest/cecile-mclorin-salvant.listen: Notice how she changes roles with her voice, like an actress.

artiest/cecilia-bartoli.text:
Cecilia Bartoli is an Italian mezzo-soprano, born in 1966 in Rome. She is known for her interpretations of the music of Bellini, Handel, Mozart, Rossini and Vivaldi and of lesser-known work from the Baroque and Classical periods. Her parents, Silvana Bazzoni and Pietro Angelo Bartoli, were professional singers and her first teachers. At nine she sang in public for the first time, as the shepherd boy in Tosca. Later she studied at the Conservatorio di Santa Cecilia in Rome. At nineteen she sang on an Italian television show and was asked to take part in a tribute to Maria Callas with the Paris Opéra.

In 1987 she made her professional opera debut at the Arena di Verona. The following year she sang Rosina in Rossini's Il barbiere di Siviglia in Cologne, Schwetzingen and Zürich, to glowing reviews. With conductors such as Daniel Barenboim and Nikolaus Harnoncourt she focused on Mozart, such as Zerlina in Don Giovanni and Dorabella in Così fan tutte. In 1990 she made her debut as Cherubino at the Opéra Bastille and in 1991 at La Scala, where her name was established as one of the best Rossini singers. In 1996 her debut at the Metropolitan Opera followed. Her recordings range from Rossini Arias in 1989 to Mozart Portraits in 1994 and An Italian Songbook in 1997.

Bartoli is regarded as a singer with an unusual sound, with full depth, a vibrant middle register and a bright, powerful top. She broke through to a large audience and made early music popular again.
artiest/cecilia-bartoli.listen: Listen to an aria from Rossini Arias or Mozart Arias and notice how fast and precisely she sings the notes. Hear how she joins heavier low notes and light high notes with a single voice.

artiest/celia-cruz.text:
Celia Caridad Cruz Alfonso (1925 to 2003) was a Cuban-American singer and one of the most popular Latin artists of the twentieth century. In the 1950s she became famous in Cuba as a singer of guarachas, which earned her the nickname La Guarachera de Cuba. For fifteen years, from 1950 to 1965, she was the singer of the group Sonora Matancera. She mastered many Afro-Cuban styles, such as guaracha, rumba, son and bolero, and recorded many singles in those styles for Seeco Records.

In 1960 she left Cuba after the Cuban Revolution had nationalised the music industry. She became a symbol and spokeswoman of the Cuban community in exile, working first in Mexico and then in the United States. In the 1960s she recorded Bemba colorá with Tito Puente, her signature song. In the 1970s she signed with Fania Records, became closely associated with salsa and had hits such as Quimbara. She often performed with the Fania All-Stars and collaborated with Johnny Pacheco and Willie Colón. La vida es un carnaval and La negra tiene tumbao followed later, as well as a Guantanamera with Wyclef Jean and Lauryn Hill. She made 37 studio albums and won two Grammy Awards and three Latin Grammy Awards.

Cruz became known as the Queen of Salsa. Her cry Azúcar! is one of the most recognisable shouts in Latin music, and her powerful, warm voice carries the rhythms of Caribbean dance music.
artiest/celia-cruz.listen: Listen to La vida es un carnaval and notice her voice and the reply of the chorus. Hear how singing and percussion alternate and how the call and response drive the song forward.

artiest/celia-cruz-en-johnny-pacheco.text:
Johnny Pacheco was born in 1935 in Santiago de los Caballeros in the Dominican Republic and moved with his family to New York at the age of eleven. His father led the big band Orquesta Santa Cecilia. As a child Pacheco learned many instruments, studied percussion at the Juilliard School and played percussion in orchestras such as those of Tito Puente and Xavier Cugat. In the 1960s he became a leading figure in New York salsa as founder and musical director of Fania Records. He popularised the word salsa and founded the Fania All-Stars to showcase the best artists of the genre.

Pacheco was also one of the forerunners of the pachanga, a blend of Cuban rhythms and Dominican merengue from the late 1950s. He died in 2021, and in 2005 received a Latin Grammy for his lifetime achievement. Celia Cruz was the Cuban singer who is regarded as the queen of salsa. Together they recorded the album Celia & Johnny in 1974, which includes Quimbara.

Salsa blends Cuban son and other rhythms with jazz and the energy of New York. Quimbara shows what that music sounds like: tight percussion, sharp brass and a big, clear voice that engages in a call-and-response game with the chorus. The duo belongs among the makers who made Latin American music popular worldwide.
artiest/celia-cruz-en-johnny-pacheco.listen: Listen to Quimbara. Notice how the singer and the chorus alternate in a call-and-response game, and how the percussion and the brass seem to keep pushing the tempo higher.

artiest/celine-dion.text:
Céline Dion is a Canadian singer, born in 1968 in Charlemagne, Quebec, into a large family. She was discovered by her later manager and husband René Angélil and became a teen star in her own country in the 1980s, with eight French-language albums. She broke through internationally by winning the Eurovision Song Contest for Switzerland in 1988 with Ne partez pas sans moi. She then made twelve English-language albums, including The Colour of My Love in 1993, Falling Into You in 1996, Let's Talk About Love in 1997 and A New Day Has Come in 2002.

She became known for theme songs for films: Beauty and the Beast for the Disney film from 1991, Because You Loved Me for Up Close & Personal in 1996 and My Heart Will Go On for Titanic in 1997, one of the best-selling singles ever. In between the English albums she continued to release French-language records. D'eux from 1995 became the best-selling French-language album. As a live performer she held the Let's Talk About Love tour and the residency A New Day in Las Vegas, the most lucrative concert series at a single venue. In 2022 she cancelled her Courage World Tour after a diagnosis of stiff-person syndrome.

Dion is called the Queen of Power Ballads. She is known for powerful, technically accomplished singing and is the best-selling Canadian artist and the best-selling French-language artist. She won five Grammy Awards and twenty Juno Awards.
artiest/celine-dion.listen: Listen to My Heart Will Go On and notice how the singing begins softly, almost whispering, and gradually grows. Hear the modulation that makes the final chorus sound a step higher still.

artiest/cesar-cui.text:
César Cui (1835 to 1918) was a Russian composer and music critic, a member of The Five, the group of composers who wanted to create a specifically Russian music, and of the Belyayev circle. He was born in Vilnius, then part of the Russian Empire, the youngest of five children in a Catholic family of French and Polish-Lithuanian descent. His French father had come to Russia with Napoleon's army and was wounded at Smolensk. As a child Cui spoke French, Polish, Russian and Lithuanian and in 1850 he was given music lessons by Stanisław Moniuszko.

He was sent to Saint Petersburg, attended the Main Engineering School and in 1857 began his military career as a lecturer in fortification. His pupils included members of the imperial family, among them Nicholas II. He became a general of engineers and wrote several monographs about his subject. Alongside that work he continued to compose and to write about music. His catalogue contains many songs and piano pieces, including 25 Preludes, opus 64, Kaleidoscope, opus 50, a violin sonata in D, opus 86, and the opera A Feast in Time of Plague. He also wrote Suite Concertante and a series of suites for orchestra.

His music is small in scale and lyrical and has a French flavour. Cui shows how an officer with a busy profession, as critic and composer, helped to build a national Russian musical style.
artiest/cesar-cui.listen: Listen to one of the 25 Preludes, opus 64, on piano. Notice the short, song-like pieces and how each prelude holds on to a single mood.

artiest/cesar-zuiderwijk.text:
Cesar Zuiderwijk is a Dutch drummer, born in 1948 in The Hague as Cornelis Johannes Zuiderwijk. At twelve he began with the guitar; two years later he switched to drums. His father died when he was a teenager, and drumming became, he said, the best way to get rid of his pent-up anger. He played in a school band, in Hu & the Hilltops and in Livin' Blues.

In 1970 the Hague rock band Golden Earring asked him to succeed the drummer Sieb Warner. From that moment the band, apart from short periods, consisted of the same four friends: Zuiderwijk, George Kooymans, Barry Hay and Rinus Gerritsen. With Radar Love from 1973 the group reached number 1 in the Netherlands and also scored in England and America. Twilight Zone followed in 1982 and When the Lady Smiles in 1984. In total Golden Earring had almost thirty top-ten hits in the Netherlands.

On stage Zuiderwijk was a striking presence. At every concert he played a drum solo that he ended by jumping over his drum kit. Together with the bassist Gerritsen he formed the solid rhythm section on which the band thrived. After Golden Earring he gave drum lessons and opened a music school in Rotterdam. In 1992 he played Radar Love with the band and a thousand other drummers on the Maasvlakte. In 2021 Golden Earring stopped because of the serious illness of Kooymans.
artiest/cesar-zuiderwijk.listen: Listen to Radar Love by Golden Earring. Notice how Zuiderwijk's drums, together with the bass, set the pace of a car on the motorway, and the long drum passage in the middle.

artiest/chaka-khan.text:
Chaka Khan is the stage name of Yvette Marie Stevens, an American singer and songwriter, born in 1953 in Chicago. She grew up in the Hyde Park district on the south side of the city. Her career began in the early 1970s as lead singer of the funk band Rufus. With the band she had hits such as Tell Me Something Good, Sweet Thing, Do You Love What You Feel and the platinum Ain't Nobody. Albums by the group include Rags to Rufus in 1974, Rufusized in 1974 and Ask Rufus in 1977.

Her solo debut Chaka from 1978 contained I'm Every Woman, a number one on the R&B chart and later a pop success for Whitney Houston. What Cha' Gonna Do for Me followed, and in 1984 her version of Prince's I Feel for You, with which she became the first R&B artist to have a crossover hit with a rapper. Through the Fire is also among her hits. In 1986 she made Higher Love with Steve Winwood, a number one on the Billboard Hot 100. She worked with, among others, Ry Cooder, Ray Charles, Quincy Jones, Miles Davis, Chick Corea and Joni Mitchell, and received eleven Grammys, including a Lifetime Achievement Award. In 2023 she was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

Khan is called the Queen of Funk. Her voice is powerful, agile and full of soul, and she shows how funk, R&B, pop and jazz come together in a single voice.
artiest/chaka-khan.listen: Listen to I Feel for You and notice her voice and the rap in between. Hear how the repeated name in the chorus is given an electronic, danceable rhythm.

artiest/chamber-orchestra-of-europe.text:
The Chamber Orchestra of Europe, COE for short, was founded in 1981 and has its office in London. The idea came from musicians in the European Community Youth Orchestra who had become too old for that youth orchestra but wanted to carry on playing in a chamber orchestra. Among the founders was the oboist Douglas Boyd. The orchestra has about sixty members from all over Europe. They combine orchestral work with a career as soloists, in chamber music groups and as teachers. The COE has no permanent hall and no permanent chief conductor, but has worked closely for years with conductors such as Claudio Abbado, Bernard Haitink and Nikolaus Harnoncourt.

On record the orchestra made itself widely heard from the mid-1980s. In 1984 Serenade for Strings in E appeared, followed by, among others, Symphonies 40 & 41 Jupiter in 1985, Le quattro stagioni in 1987 and, in 1989 and 1990, whole series of symphonies. The orchestra made more than two hundred and fifty recordings and won, among other awards, two Grammys. It was also the first orchestra with its own label, COE Records.

The sound is that of a flexible chamber orchestra: light, transparent and with strong soloists in the ranks. The COE plays in the great concert halls of Europe and between 2007 and 2013 was given the role of cultural ambassador of the European Union. In 2009 it also started its own academy for talented students. The orchestra shows how a group of like-minded musicians, without a permanent conductor or home, can build an interpretive style of its own.
artiest/chamber-orchestra-of-europe.listen: Listen to a recording of Symphonies 40 & 41 Jupiter and notice how transparent the strings and winds sound. Try to hear how the separate voices together form one light sound, without the orchestra becoming heavy.
